# Fisher information and the geometry of memorization in neural networks

A fruitful approach towards understanding generalization in machine learning involves characterizing how models separate generalizable structure from idiosyncratic or even corrupted features of training data. Fisher information has emerged as a diagnostic tool for this separation, leveraging loss geometry to distinguish generalization from memorization. Here we investigate this connection in vision models trained on CIFAR-10 with controlled noise that can be learned only through memorization. We show that projecting model weights onto the top Fisher eigenvectors decouples general task performance from noisy sample memorization, and we investigate how this decoupling presents differentially across layers. We show that the same phenomena are present in small transformers trained to solve a synthetic in-context learning task, and are reproduced in closed form in a simple, analytically solvable linear model. Our results reveal that Fisher information captures aspects of the geometric structure underlying how neural networks allocate capacity between

Modern neural networks can memorize their training set [1], yet in practice they learn features that generalize to unseen examples. Disentangling memorization from generalization is a central problem in machine learning—large language models reproduce substantial fractions of their pretraining data [2], raising copyright and privacy concerns; adversaries can exploit memorization through data poisoning [3]; and memorization of mislabeled examples degrades generalization. Progress on any of these fronts requires a clearer picture of how trained models store memorized content and what distinguishes it from generalizing features. The geometry of the loss landscape offers a natural setting for this question, and recent work argues that the eigenspectrum of the Fisher information separates memorized information from generalizing features, using this separation to remove memorized content from trained language models [4]. Here, we investigate this phenomenon across several settings designed to probe how and when the Fisher

The Fisher information’s averaging structure suggests why it might isolate memorization. On a dataset D, the Fisher decomposes as an average of per-sample contributions, F = 1 |D| P x∈D Fx, where each Fx measures the sensitivity of the network’s output to its parameters at sample x. Directions that encode generalizing features should align across single-sample Fishers and add coherently in this *DTB and CG contributed to this work equally. §VN and DJS contributed to this work equally. 1Lewis-Sigler Institute 2 Joseph Henry Laboratories 3 School of Physics 4 Initiative for the Theoretical Sciences

average. On the other hand, directions that encode memorization of particular samples should instead be largely orthogonal in parameter space and suppressed by a factor ~1/|D| in the average. The top of the population Fisher’s eigenspectrum is therefore a natural place to look for a separation between memorized content and generalizing structure. This picture turns memorization into a set of testable geometric predictions. If memorized features are supported on sample-specific directions, then projecting onto the top Fisher eigenspaces should preserve structure shared across the training distribution while suppressing information tied to individual examples. In a trained network, however, the relevant eigenspaces may depend on the data used to compute the Fisher, may appear only in particular layers, and may trade off memorization removal against the loss of weak but useful features. These considerations motivate our experiments. The Gaussian-image setting isolates pure input-level memorization (§3.1), the label-noise setting tests whether de-memorization can recover an underlying correct label (§3.2) and the in-context regression setting asks whether the same geometry applies to memorized latent tasks (§3.3). The barcode model then distills the same mechanism into a linear setting where finite-sample correlations with uninformative features can be analyzed in closed form (§5). Our work extends this Fisher-based account of memorization in three directions. First, we show that distinct forms of memorized content—random-input examples, mislabeled training examples, and memorized latent tasks in a synthetic in-context learning task—leave distinct signatures in the layer-wise Fisher geometry. Second, we find that the geometric separation between memorization and generalization depends sharply on the data used to evaluate the Fisher: a denoised dataset yields cleaner separation than the full training distribution. Third, suppressing memorized directions can partially recover task generalization that the trained model otherwise loses to overfitting.

In this work, we study the relationship between sample memorization and the Fisher information. We do so by investigating conditions under which the projection of a neural network’s weights onto a subspace governed by the Fisher information induces de-memorization. We define de-memorization as an operation performed on a neural network which disproportionately degrades its performance on samples that the network was forced to memorize, while inducing only minor degradation on other samples. We emphasize that de-memorization is separate from the phenomenon of unlearning: de-memorization does not allow a network to selectively forget individual samples in its training set [5–7]. We specify the projection operation in detail in the Experiments section. Our contributions are

• We demonstrate how low-eigenvalue subspaces of the Fisher information encode memorized data across a variety of experimental settings: We investigate input/output noise in image classifiers, the structure of subspaces across layers, and an in-context regression task. • We show that de-memorization performance depends on the samples used to compute the Fisher: the structure of Fisher eigenspaces with respect to memorization is data-dependent. • In an in-context regression problem, we demonstrate that de-memorization can be lifted to the level of latent tasks while simultaneously improving task generalization, and we identify model components responsible for task memorization. • We investigate how easily individual samples can be de-memorized from the model by using information encoded in single-sample Fisher matrices, and we use the language of participation ratios to understand how different kinds of samples contribute to different regions of the eigenspectrum. • We develop an analytically tractable “barcode” model that exhibits the de-memorization phenomenon in a simple linear setting.

Curvature-based signatures of memorization. Recent works have used local curvature measures to identify example-level memorization. Most closely related to our work, Merullo et al. [4] study the eigenspectrum of loss curvature in language models, finding that the top Fisher modes encode reasoning-like structure, whereas lower-curvature modes encode memorized samples. Influence-function methods use gradients and Hessian-vector products to map predictions back to influential training examples

Memorization and noisy labels. Overparameterized neural networks can fit arbitrary labels and random inputs [1]. However, networks also tend to learn simple, “shared” structure before fitting noisy samples [10], which has inspired methods that can leverage this tendency to train networks on very noisy data [11]. Memorization can also be beneficial for generalization, and influencebased approaches suggest that memorization of atypical examples can improve performance on rare

Loss geometry, sharpness, and Fisher information. A significant body of work relates generalization to the local geometry of the loss landscape. Flatter minima have long been hypothesized to generalize better [14], and empirical studies have connected sharp minima to generalization gaps [15, 16]. Studies of the Hessian spectrum have shown that trained networks typically exhibit a small set of stiff directions along with a bulk of near-zero eigenvalues [17–19]. The Fisher information provides a related local metric [20, 21] which does not rely on a loss function to measure model sensitivity. Furthermore, there is evidence that flat directions connect minima more globally [22–25]. Fisher information has been used to identify parameter directions important for previously learned tasks in continual learning [26] and to study early phase training dynamics [27]. In-context learning and task overfitting. Regression tasks have become a standard testbed for studying in-context learning [28–30]. More recent work shows that the emergence of in-context learning depends strongly on task diversity and training duration, such that transformers may first generalize to held-out tasks and later overfit by memorizing the finite set of training tasks [31–33]. Further work localizes the memorization to the MLP layers in the transformer [32, 33]. Benign overfitting and data coarse-graining. Our theoretical model studies a simplified setting of high-dimensional linear regression. In work on benign overfitting [34, 35], fitting pure noise can increase variance, and removing uninformative feature directions after fitting can reduce risk in finite samples. Our model isolates a “barcode” block that is uninformative across the population but is correlated with potential label noise. Data coarse-graining work shows that discarding data dimensions can improve predictive performance when the discarded degrees of freedom primarily

Unlearning. The de-memorization phenomena we study is distinct from unlearning research. Unlearning refers to the procedure of forcing a neural network to forget specific information on which it was trained, and is usually studied in the context of data privacy concerns or data which might produce harmful behavior in the model [5–7]. The type of model editing that we investigate does not support fine-grained deletion of information required for unlearning.

To explore the interplay between memorization and loss geometry, we force models to memorize a subset of their training data using two variants of the standard CIFAR-10 classification task [37]. First, to study input noise, we augment the CIFAR-10 training set with 500 synthetic images (1% of the training set). Following standard protocols for injected noise (see, e.g., Ref [1]), each synthetic image is drawn from a Gaussian distribution whose mean and variance match the statistics of a randomly chosen CIFAR-10 class, but is assigned the label of an independently chosen random class. Because the input statistics and labels are independent, the network cannot rely on generalizable features, forcing it to explicitly memorize these inputs. Second, to study label noise, we randomly corrupt 10% of the training labels (see, e.g., Ref [8]). Each corrupted label is reassigned uniformly among the nine incorrect classes, forcing the network to explicitly memorize these modified samples. In both settings, we train a ResNet-20 [38] to 100% training accuracy (details in Appendix A.1). Following Merullo et al. [4], we compute and diagonalize each layer’s Fisher information matrix and

We compute the Fisher information over the entire training set, including both CIFAR

In the first layer, the model’s accuracy on standard CIFAR-10 images (both train and test) rises quickly as a function of the eigenspace dimension k, outpacing its accuracy on the Gaussian data. At an eigenspace dimension of k≈ 45, the model achieves near-maximum accuracy on the CIFAR-10 dataset while correctly classifying less than 30% of the Gaussian samples. The accuracy on both the CIFAR-10 train and test sets rises in tandem, showing that this procedure separates the memorized data distribution from the learned distribution of CIFAR-10 images. Applying this projection to the final layer results in markedly different behavior. Accuracy across all three partitions (CIFAR-10 train, CIFAR-10 test and Gaussian) climbs simultaneously to full-model accuracy as the subspace dimension k increases. By this layer, the model’s representations of the two data distributions have converged, precluding selective removal. Taken together with the first layer, this indicates that the signature of memorization is layer-dependent, restricting de-memorization interventions to specific layers. We also note that nearly all the relevant predictive information in the final layer’s weights is concentrated within the span of the top ~5% of its eigendirections.

We next investigate memorization in an in-context learning (ICL) setting [39]. A growing body of work has developed in-context learning of linear regression as a simple model of ICL amenable to quantitative study [28, 31, 40, 41]. One important feature of ICL captured by the linear regression model is that ICL behavior can be transient, emerging early on during training before the model memorizes the set of training tasks [31–33]. We train a three-block GPT-2 style transformer on contexts Cτ =(x1,y1,x2,y2,...,xn) with yi = wT τxi. The model must learn to effectively infer the latent regression “task” vector wτ to predict yn. Following Ref [31], training contexts are sampled uniformly from a set of M task vectors, {wτ}M τ=1. As shown in Fig 4A, when M is small, performance on held-out tasks first improves until the model overfits to the training tasks. We next compute the Fisher information for each component in the model, and project the model parameters onto top-k subspaces. In Fig 4B and C, we show the results for the second transformer block’s attention and MLP layers (See Appendix Fig 8 for all layers). We see that in the attention layer, projecting onto top subspace only hurts model performance, on both the memorized training tasks and held-out test tasks. However, the same projection procedure applied to the MLP layer yields a substantial improvement in test performance at the cost of performance on the memorized tasks. We note that prior work also identified the MLP as the component of a transformer responsible for memorization [32, 33]; our analysis further suggests that this memorized information is stored in low-Fisher-eigenvalue parameter components. 4 Contributions of Individual Samples 4.1 Sample Contributions to the Eigenspectrum To better understand how individual data samples contribute to generalization and the structure of the Fisher information, we examine the participation ratios associated with individual samples in the eigenspectrum of the (layerwise) Fisher. To get some intuition, we can express the Fisher information as an average over per-sample Fishers: 1 n Pn i=1 Fi. Then, diagonalizing the Fisher as F = Pp k=1 λkfiukfiu⊺ k , we define the contribution of sample i to mode k as ck i = fiu⊺ kFifiuk. The participation ratio for mode k is then Ψk =(P ick i)2/(nP i (ck i)2). This ratio is a measure of the fraction of data samples that contribute to mode k. For example, when ck i = 1 for all i, Ψk = 1 and all samples contribute (equally). On the other hand, when only a single sample contributes, Ψk = 1 n and the participation ratio is suppressed by the size of the dataset. The restricted participation ratio Ψk CIFAR ≡(P j∈CIFAR ck j)2/(nP i (ck i)2) restricts the numerator to only the contributions of the CIFAR samples, and this convention is used equivalently for Ψk Gauss,Ψk corrupted, and Ψk uncorrupted. Note thatΨk ≠Ψk CIFAR +Ψk Gauss generically because of cross-terms. Figure 5A and B display first-layer participation ratios across the eigenspectrum. In the input-noise experiments (Fig 5A), we see total participation ratios drop by roughly one order of magnitude from top to bottom modes. Importantly, the restricted ratios show that clean CIFAR-10 images dominate the top modes, whereas memorized Gaussian noise is relegated to the bottom. These findings suggest that the top eigenmodes capture information about structured, generalizing features in the data, while the bottom portion corresponds to memorized, idiosyncratic information. By contrast, in the noisy-label experiments (Fig 5B), we see that corrupted and uncorrupted samples contribute in a constant ratio across the entire spectrum.
